claim: Gonorrhea is caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
source: Gonorrhea, which is caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, is the second most reported sexually transmitted infection worldwide.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and introduction.

claim: Gonorrhea is the second most reported sexually transmitted infection worldwide.
source: Gonorrhea, which is caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, is the second most reported sexually transmitted infection worldwide.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and introduction.

claim: Approximately 82.4 million new adult gonorrhea infections occurred globally in 2020.
source: According to the World Health Organization (WHO) approximately 82.4 million new adult gonorrhea infections occurred globally in 2020 (WHO, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to WHO, 2019.

claim: The high dose (500 mg) of the cephalosporin ceftriaxone is currently the only recommended therapy for treating gonorrhea infections in the USA.
source: The high dose (500 mg) of the cephalosporin ceftriaxone is currently the only recommended therapy for treating gonorrhea infections in the USA (St Cyr et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to St Cyr et al., 2020.

claim: There are growing instances of drug resistant N. gonorrhoeae 'superbugs'.
source: The growing instances of drug resistant 'superbugs', together with the limited clinical treatment options, underscore the urgent need for additional antibiotics that target N. gonorrhoeae (Unemo et al., 2012; Ohnishi et al., 2011; Day et al., 2022; Derbie et al., 2020; Sawatzky et al., 2022; Shaskolskiy et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: There is an urgent need for additional antibiotics that target N. gonorrhoeae.
source: The growing instances of drug resistant 'superbugs', together with the limited clinical treatment options, underscore the urgent need for additional antibiotics that target N. gonorrhoeae (Unemo et al., 2012; Ohnishi et al., 2011; Day et al., 2022; Derbie et al., 2020; Sawatzky et al., 2022; Shaskolskiy et al., 2022).
evidence: This is inferred from the growing drug resistance and limited treatment options, supported by citations.

claim: Bacterial natural products inspired the development of both ceftriaxone and azithromycin.
source: The characterization of antibacterial active natural products inspired the development of both ceftriaxone and azithromycin (Richards et al., 1984; Bakheit et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Richards et al., 1984 and Bakheit et al., 2014.

claim: Bacterial natural products have been a key source of antibiotics with diverse modes of action.
source: Bacterial natural products have been a key source of antibiotics with diverse modes of action and the most fruitful source of therapeutically useful antibiotics (Newman and Cragg, 2020; Dias et al., 2012; Lewis, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Newman and Cragg, 2020; Dias et al., 2012; Lewis, 2020.

claim: Bacterial natural products are the most fruitful source of therapeutically useful antibiotics.
source: Bacterial natural products have been a key source of antibiotics with diverse modes of action and the most fruitful source of therapeutically useful antibiotics (Newman and Cragg, 2020; Dias et al., 2012; Lewis, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Newman and Cragg, 2020; Dias et al., 2012; Lewis, 2020.

claim: Oxydifficidin was serendipitously identified as a potent N. gonorrhoeae active antibiotic.
source: Here, we describe the serendipitous identification of the natural product oxydifficidin (Wilson et al., 1987; Zimmerman et al., 1987) as a potent N. gonorrhoeae active antibiotic and show that this activity arises from a combination of DedA flippase-assisted uptake and ribosomal protein L7/L12 (RplL) sensitivity.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Oxydifficidin's activity arises from a combination of DedA flippase-assisted uptake and ribosomal protein L7/L12 (RplL) sensitivity.
source: Here, we describe the serendipitous identification of the natural product oxydifficidin (Wilson et al., 1987; Zimmerman et al., 1987) as a potent N. gonorrhoeae active antibiotic and show that this activity arises from a combination of DedA flippase-assisted uptake and ribosomal protein L7/L12 (RplL) sensitivity.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data on DedA and RplL mutations.

claim: Oxydifficidin provides a new therapeutic lead structure for addressing the growing problem of antibiotic resistant gonorrhea.
source: Oxydifficidin provides a new therapeutic lead structure for addressing the growing problem of antibiotic resistant gonorrhea.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing oxydifficidin's potent activity against multidrug-resistant N. gonorrhoeae.

claim: Metabolites with specific potent activity against historically less problematic pathogens may have been overlooked in past antibiotic screens.
source: This study suggests that reexamining cultured bacteria for antibiotics active against today's emerging pathogens may be fruitful as metabolites with specific potent activity against historically less problematic pathogens may have been overlooked.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the discovery of oxydifficidin's specific activity against N. gonorrhoeae.

claim: A Bacillus amyloliquefaciens contaminant was observed on a lawn of N. gonorrhoeae surrounded by a zone of growth inhibition.
source: On one lawn of N. gonorrhoeae we observed an environmental contaminant that was surrounded by a zone of growth inhibition suggesting that it produced an anti-N. gonorrhoeae metabolite (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is an observation documented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The contaminant did not produce a zone of growth inhibition against E. coli, V. cholerae, or C. crescentus.
source: When we screened this contaminant for antibacterial activity against lawns of other Gram-negative bacteria it did not produce a zone of growth of inhibition against any of the bacteria we tested (e.g., Escherichia coli, Vibrio cholerae, Caulobacter crescentus).
evidence: This is experimental data from screening the contaminant against other bacteria.

claim: The contaminant was most closely related to Bacillus amyloliquefaciens based on genome sequencing and clustering analysis.
source: Sequencing of the contaminant's genome and genome clustering analysis (Appendix 1—figure 1a) revealed that it was most closely related to Bacillus amyloliquefaciens, which is a root-colonizing bacterium that is used as a biocontrol agent (Ngalimat et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on genomic sequencing data and phylogenetic analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 1a.

claim: Bacillus amyloliquefaciens is a root-colonizing bacterium that is used as a biocontrol agent.
source: Sequencing of the contaminant's genome and genome clustering analysis (Appendix 1—figure 1a) revealed that it was most closely related to Bacillus amyloliquefaciens, which is a root-colonizing bacterium that is used as a biocontrol agent (Ngalimat et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Ngalimat et al., 2021.

claim: The non-producer strain of B. amyloliquefaciens BK contained four transposon insertions and one frame shift mutation.
source: The sequencing of the non-producer strain revealed that it surprisingly contained four transposon insertions and one frame shift mutation (Appendix 1—figure 1b).
evidence: This is genomic sequencing data from the mutant strain shown in Appendix 1—figure 1b.

claim: The transposon was inserted into the bacillomycin (mycosubtilin) BGC.
source: The transposon inserted into the bacillomycin (mycosubtilin) BGC, while the frame shift mutation was predicted to disrupt the (oxy)difficidin BGC.
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis of the transposon insertion sites.

claim: The frame shift mutation was predicted to disrupt the (oxy)difficidin BGC.
source: The transposon inserted into the bacillomycin (mycosubtilin) BGC, while the frame shift mutation was predicted to disrupt the (oxy)difficidin BGC.
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis and prediction of the mutation's effect.

claim: Only disruption of the (oxy)difficidin BGC eliminated the anti-N. gonorrhoeae activity.
source: Only disruption of the (oxy)difficidin BGC eliminated the anti-N. gonorrhoeae activity (Appendix 1—figure 1c).
evidence: This is experimental data from testing targeted BGC disruptions shown in Appendix 1—figure 1c.

claim: HRMS and NMR data from the major active peak were consistent with it being an oxydifficidin isomer.
source: High-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS) and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) data from the major active peak we isolated were consistent with its being an oxydifficidin isomer (Figure 1b, Appendix 1—figures 5–12, and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on analytical chemistry data (HRMS and NMR) shown in figures.

claim: Oxydifficidin contains a 27-carbon polyketide backbone that is cyclized through a terminal carboxylic acid and an oxidation at position 21.
source: Oxydifficidin contains a 27-carbon polyketide backbone that is cyclized through a terminal carboxylic acid and an oxidation at position 21.
evidence: This is structural characterization based on NMR and HRMS data.

claim: Oxydifficidin's hydrophobic core is phosphorylated at C16.
source: This hydrophobic core is phosphorylated at C16.
evidence: This is structural characterization based on NMR and HRMS data.

claim: Oxydifficidin occurs naturally as a collection of interconverting thermal isomers.
source: Oxydifficidin occurs naturally as a collection of interconverting thermal isomers (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is based on observations and previous reports cited in the manuscript.

claim: An interconversion of isomers was observed with the compound purified from B. amyloliquefaciens BK cultures.
source: As reported previously, we observed an interconversion of isomers with the compound we purified from B. amyloliquefaciens BK cultures (Wilson et al., 1987; Zimmerman et al., 1987).
evidence: This is experimental observation consistent with previous reports cited.

claim: Oxydifficidin showed only weak activity against most pathogens.
source: Oxydifficidin showed only weak activity against most pathogens, however we observed potent activity against N. gonorrhoeae (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is based on MIC testing data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Oxydifficidin showed potent activity against N. gonorrhoeae.
source: Oxydifficidin showed only weak activity against most pathogens, however we observed potent activity against N. gonorrhoeae (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is based on MIC testing data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Oxydifficidin was consistently more active against Neisseria than any of the other bacteria tested.
source: When we examined other Neisseria species, we found that oxydifficidin was consistently more active against Neisseria than any of the other bacteria we tested.
evidence: This is based on MIC testing data across multiple bacterial species.

claim: Among Neisseria spp., oxydifficidin was most active against N. gonorrhoeae.
source: Among Neisseria spp., oxydifficidin was most active against N. gonorrhoeae underscoring a unique narrow spectrum of potent activity.
evidence: This is based on MIC testing data across Neisseria species shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Oxydifficidin was more potent against N. gonorrhoeae MS11 than most other antibiotics tested.
source: Oxydifficidin was more potent against N. gonorrhoeae MS11 than most other antibiotics we tested.
evidence: This is based on comparative MIC data shown in Table 1.

claim: Oxydifficidin retained activity against all multidrug-resistant clinical isolates examined.
source: Notably, unlike clinically used antibiotics such as ceftriaxone, azithromycin, and ciprofloxacin, oxydifficidin retained activity against all multidrug-resistant clinical isolates we examined (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on MIC testing data against resistant strains shown in Table 1.

claim: Ceftriaxone, azithromycin, and ciprofloxacin did not retain activity against all multidrug-resistant clinical isolates examined.
source: Notably, unlike clinically used antibiotics such as ceftriaxone, azithromycin, and ciprofloxacin, oxydifficidin retained activity against all multidrug-resistant clinical isolates we examined (Table 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison with oxydifficidin and supported by MIC data in Table 1.

claim: Only one resistant mutant appeared from >1.5 × 10^10 N. gonorrhoeae cells screened on oxydifficidin-containing plates.
source: Out of the >1.5 × 1010 cells we screened, only one resistant mutant appeared.
evidence: This is experimental data from the resistance mutation screening.

claim: Oxydifficidin's MIC against the resistant mutant increased by eightfold (2 μg/ml).
source: Oxydifficidin's MIC against this mutant increased by eightfold (2 μg/ml).
evidence: This is MIC testing data from the resistant mutant.

claim: No increase in MIC was observed for any other antibiotic tested against the resistant mutant.
source: No increase in MIC was observed for any other antibiotic we tested (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is MIC testing data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The resistant mutant contained a single mutation that introduced a frame shift in one of the three predicted dedA genes in N. gonorrhoeae MS11.
source: Sequencing and comparison of this mutant's genome to the sensitive parent genome revealed a single mutation that introduced a frame shift in one of the three predicted dedA genes found in the N. gonorrhoeae MS11 (NCBI:txid528354 dedA NGFG_RS04905; Jen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is genomic sequencing data from the resistant mutant.

claim: A dedA deletion mutant showed an eightfold increase in oxydifficidin's MIC.
source: This mutant showed the same eightfold increase in oxydifficidin's MIC, confirming that the deletion of dedA is sufficient to reduce oxydifficidin's potent activity.
evidence: This is MIC testing data from the engineered deletion mutant.

claim: The deletion of dedA is sufficient to reduce oxydifficidin's potent activity.
source: This mutant showed the same eightfold increase in oxydifficidin's MIC, confirming that the deletion of dedA is sufficient to reduce oxydifficidin's potent activity.
evidence: This is confirmed by MIC testing of the engineered deletion mutant.

claim: Deletion mutants for two other predicted dedA-like genes showed the same MIC as the N. gonorrhoeae MS11 wild-type strain.
source: We also generated deletion mutants for two other predicted dedA-like genes, and the MIC of oxydifficidin for these mutants remained the same as for the N. gonorrhoeae MS11 wild-type (WT) strain.
evidence: This is MIC testing data from deletion mutants of other dedA-like genes.

claim: DedA deficient N. gonorrhoeae is less susceptible to oxydifficidin.
source: Interestingly, not only was dedA deficient N. gonorrhoeae less susceptible to oxydifficidin, oxydifficidin also kills this mutant more slowly (Figure 2b) than WT N. gonorrhoeae MS11.
evidence: This is based on MIC and time-kill assay data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Oxydifficidin kills dedA deficient N. gonorrhoeae more slowly than WT N. gonorrhoeae MS11.
source: Interestingly, not only was dedA deficient N. gonorrhoeae less susceptible to oxydifficidin, oxydifficidin also kills this mutant more slowly (Figure 2b) than WT N. gonorrhoeae MS11.
evidence: This is based on time-kill assay data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The dedA deletion mutant showed altered cell morphology with reduced membrane integrity and lower formation of microcolonies.
source: The dedA deletion mutant also showed an altered cell morphology with reduced membrane integrity and lower formation of microcolonies (Appendix 1—figures 4).
evidence: This is based on microscopy data shown in Appendix 1—figures 4.

claim: A survey of 220 N. gonorrhoeae strains with high-quality assemblies in NCBI found no mutations in the DedA protein.
source: A survey of 220 N. gonorrhoeae strains with high-quality assemblies in NCBI found no mutations in the DedA protein.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis of genomic databases.

claim: The DedA protein superfamily is highly conserved, with examples in almost every sequenced genome across all domains of life.
source: The DedA protein superfamily is highly conserved, with examples in almost every sequenced genome across all domains of life (Doerrler et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Doerrler et al., 2013.

claim: DedA family members are predicted to be transmembrane proteins with still largely, poorly defined, functions.
source: DedA family members are predicted to be transmembrane proteins with still largely, poorly defined, functions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DedA proteins.

claim: DedA homologs are flippases that flip phospholipids or phospholipid-like structures across prokaryotic and eukaryotic lipid bilayers.
source: However, a few recent studies indicate that DedA homologs are flippases. They have been reported to flip phospholipids (phosphatidylethanolamine, phosphatidylserine) or phospholipid-like structures (C55-isoprenyl pyrophosphate) across prokaryotic and eukaryotic lipid bilayers (Sit et al., 2023; Roney and Rudner, 2023; Huang et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies (Sit et al., 2023; Roney and Rudner, 2023; Huang et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021).

claim: Oxydifficidin's overall structure resembles that of reported DedA protein substrates, especially C55-isoprenyl pyrophosphate.
source: Although oxydifficidin is not a phospholipid, its overall structure resembles that of reported DedA protein substrates, especially C55-isoprenyl pyrophosphate (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The DedA protein associated with oxydifficidin potency is most closely related to the C55-isoprenyl pyrophosphate flippase YghB from V. cholerae.
source: Interestingly, among the two characterized bacterial family members, the DedA protein associated with oxydifficidin potency is most closely related to the C55-isoprenyl pyrophosphate flippase YghB from V. cholerae (Appendix 1—figure 2; Sit et al., 2023).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 2 and citation to Sit et al., 2023.

claim: DedA is not the direct target of oxydifficidin.
source: As oxydifficidin's activity was not completely abrogated in the dedA knockout we postulated that DedA was not the direct target of oxydifficidin, but it instead acted to increase oxydifficidin's potency in N. gonorrhoeae.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that oxydifficidin retains some activity in the dedA knockout.

claim: DedA acts to increase oxydifficidin's potency in N. gonorrhoeae.
source: As oxydifficidin's activity was not completely abrogated in the dedA knockout we postulated that DedA was not the direct target of oxydifficidin, but it instead acted to increase oxydifficidin's potency in N. gonorrhoeae.
evidence: This is inferred from MIC and time-kill data comparing WT and dedA knockout strains.

claim: DedA is responsible for assisting with oxydifficidin uptake into N. gonorrhoeae.
source: The structural similarity between oxydifficidin and the known substrates of DedA homologs led us to explore the possibility that DedA was responsible for assisting with oxydifficidin uptake into N. gonorrhoeae.
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested by accumulation assays shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Six times more oxydifficidin was found in cells from WT cultures than from dedA deletion strain cultures.
source: In the case of oxydifficidin we saw six times more antibiotic in cells from WT cultures than from dedA deletion strain cultures.
evidence: This is based on drug accumulation assay data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: For tetracycline and chloramphenicol, the ratio of antibiotic in WT vs dedA deletion cells was less than two.
source: For the other antibiotics we tested (tetracycline and chloramphenicol) this ratio was less than two.
evidence: This is based on drug accumulation assay data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: DedA flips oxydifficidin across the inner membrane to increase its cytoplasmic concentration and increase its potency against N. gonorrhoeae.
source: Based on DedA homologs flipping phospholipid-like structures across a lipid bilayer our data is consistent with DedA flipping oxydifficidin across the inner membrane to increase its cytoplasmic concentration and in turn increase its potency against N. gonorrhoeae.
evidence: This is inferred from accumulation data and knowledge of DedA function.

claim: A DedA-assisted uptake mechanism could explain the slower rate of killing observed for oxydifficidin against dedA deficient N. gonorrhoeae compared to WT N. gonorrhoeae.
source: A DedA-assisted uptake mechanism could also explain the slower rate of killing we observed for oxydifficidin against dedA deficient N. gonorrhoeae compared to WT N. gonorrhoeae.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the uptake model and time-kill data.

claim: No cell lysis or membrane depolarization was detected at even 100 times oxydifficidin's MIC.
source: While we cannot definitely rule out the possibility that DedA accumulation of oxydifficidin in the membrane could also have a direct toxicity effect, we did not detect any cell lysis or membrane depolarization at even 100 times oxydifficidin's MIC (Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: This is based on cell lysis and depolarization assay data shown in Appendix 1—figure 3.

claim: From ~1 × 10^10 dedA deletion cells plated on 8 μg/ml oxydifficidin, 12 resistant mutants were identified.
source: From ~1 × 1010 cells plated on 8 μg/ml oxydifficidin (4× MIC for N. gonorrhoeae dedA deletion strain) we identified 12 resistant mutants.
evidence: This is experimental data from the second round of resistance screening.

claim: The oxydifficidin MIC for the 12 resistant mutants increased to 16 μg/ml.
source: In each case, the oxydifficidin MIC increased to 16 μg/ml.
evidence: This is MIC testing data from the resistant mutants.

claim: Each of the 12 resistant mutants contained a point mutation in the gene encoding for the large ribosomal protein(s) L7/L12 (rplL).
source: Sequencing of these strains revealed that each contained a point mutation in the gene encoding for the large ribosomal protein(s) L7/L12 (rplL).
evidence: This is genomic sequencing data from the resistant mutants.

claim: Eleven resistant strains contained the R76C mutation in rplL and one contained a K84E mutation.
source: Eleven strains contained the same R76C mutation and one contained a K84E mutation (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is genomic sequencing data from the resistant mutants.

claim: The R76C and K84E mutations in rplL were not found in a survey of 220 N. gonorrhoeae strains.
source: These two mutations were not found in the survey of the same collection of N. gonorrhoeae strains used to look for DedA mutations.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis of genomic databases.

claim: An RplL R76C mutant in a WT N. gonorrhoeae background exhibited an eightfold increase in oxydifficidin's MIC (2 μg/ml).
source: This mutant exhibited an eightfold increase in oxydifficidin's MIC (2 μg/ml) compared to the parent strain, confirming that the R76C mutation in L7/L12 alone was sufficient to increase the MIC of oxydifficidin.
evidence: This is MIC testing data from the engineered mutant.

claim: The R76C mutation in L7/L12 alone is sufficient to increase the MIC of oxydifficidin.
source: This mutant exhibited an eightfold increase in oxydifficidin's MIC (2 μg/ml) compared to the parent strain, confirming that the R76C mutation in L7/L12 alone was sufficient to increase the MIC of oxydifficidin.
evidence: This is confirmed by MIC testing of the engineered mutant.

claim: Ribosomal proteins L7 and L12 have the same sequence, however L12 has an N-terminal acetylation.
source: Ribosomal proteins L7 and L12 have the same sequence, however L12 has an N-terminal acetylation (Diaconu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Diaconu et al., 2005.

claim: L7/L12 is part of the L10/L7 stalk of the large (50S) subunit of the bacterial ribosome.
source: L7/L12 is part of the L10/L7 stalk of the large (50S) subunit of the bacterial ribosome and is critical to a number of processes including GTP hydrolysis (Diaconu et al., 2005; Carlson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Diaconu et al., 2005 and Carlson et al., 2017.

claim: L7/L12 is critical to a number of processes including GTP hydrolysis.
source: L7/L12 is part of the L10/L7 stalk of the large (50S) subunit of the bacterial ribosome and is critical to a number of processes including GTP hydrolysis (Diaconu et al., 2005; Carlson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Diaconu et al., 2005 and Carlson et al., 2017.

claim: Oxydifficidin inhibits protein synthesis.
source: The appearance of resistance mutations in rplL suggested that oxydifficidin inhibited protein synthesis, which would be consistent with isotope feeding studies performed with difficidin and E. coli (Zweerink and Edison, 1987).
evidence: This is inferred from rplL mutations and supported by in vitro translation assays and citation to Zweerink and Edison, 1987.

claim: No protein was produced in the presence of oxydifficidin in a coupled transcription/translation system.
source: While this reaction mixture contained all the components necessary to produce a protein from DNA, no protein was produced in the presence of oxydifficidin (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is based on in vitro coupled transcription/translation assay data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Oxydifficidin does not inhibit RNA synthesis in vitro.
source: In this case we saw no inhibition of RNA synthesis, even at the highest oxydifficidin concentration we tested (13.4 μg/ml) (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is based on in vitro transcription assay data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Oxydifficidin inhibits translation but not transcription.
source: Taken together these two experiments indicate that oxydifficidin inhibits translation but not transcription and are consistent with rplL mutations providing resistance to oxydifficidin.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results of in vitro transcription and translation assays.

claim: rplL mutations have not been previously associated with antibiotic resistance.
source: To the best of our knowledge rplL mutations have not been previously associated with antibiotic resistance and no characterized antibiotics have been found to bind L7/L12.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge claim based on literature review.

claim: No characterized antibiotics have been found to bind L7/L12.
source: To the best of our knowledge rplL mutations have not been previously associated with antibiotic resistance and no characterized antibiotics have been found to bind L7/L12.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge claim based on literature review.

claim: The L7/L12 R76C mutation did not confer resistance to any other antibiotics tested.
source: When we screened for cross resistance, the L7/L12 R76C mutation did not confer resistance to any other antibiotics we tested (Table 2).
evidence: This is based on MIC testing data shown in Table 2.

claim: Tetracycline, gentamicin, and spectinomycin showed no increase in MIC with the L7/L12 R76C mutation.
source: Antibiotics that bind different regions of the 30S decoding center, including tetracycline, gentamicin, and spectinomycin showed no increase in MIC with the L7/L12 R76C mutation (Lin et al., 2018; Paternoga et al., 2023).
evidence: This is based on MIC testing data shown in Table 2 and citations to Lin et al., 2018 and Paternoga et al., 2023.

claim: The L7/L12 R76C mutation did not confer resistance to chloramphenicol or erythromycin.
source: Similarly, the L7/L12 R76C mutation did not confer resistance to chloramphenicol or erythromycin, which interact with distinct regions of the 50S peptidyl transferase center (Lin et al., 2018; Paternoga et al., 2023).
evidence: This is based on MIC testing data shown in Table 2 and citations to Lin et al., 2018 and Paternoga et al., 2023.

claim: The activity of avilamycin was not affected by the L7/L12 R76C mutation.
source: The activity of avilamycin, which binds in a unique site in the 50S subunit at the entrance to the A-site tRNA accommodating corridor was also not affected by the L7/L12 R76C mutation (Arenz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on MIC testing data shown in Table 2 and citation to Arenz et al., 2016.

claim: No change in MIC was observed for thiostrepton A with the L7/L12 R76C mutation.
source: In the case of thiostrepton A (Harms et al., 2008), which targets the L11 protein GTPase-associated center and is part of the only class of antibiotics known to bind the ribosome in the vicinity of L10/L7 stalk, we also observed no change in MIC for N. gonorrhoeae with the L7/L12 R76C mutation.
evidence: This is based on MIC testing data shown in Table 2 and citation to Harms et al., 2008.

claim: Oxydifficidin binds to a different site on the ribosome than known antibiotics.
source: The inability of the L7/L12 R76C mutation to confer cross resistance to known antibiotics suggests that oxydifficidin binds to a different site on the ribosome and that L7/L12 is uniquely associated with oxydifficidin's MOA.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of cross-resistance data shown in Table 2.

claim: L7/L12 is uniquely associated with oxydifficidin's mode of action.
source: The inability of the L7/L12 R76C mutation to confer cross resistance to known antibiotics suggests that oxydifficidin binds to a different site on the ribosome and that L7/L12 is uniquely associated with oxydifficidin's MOA.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of cross-resistance and the specific rplL mutations conferring resistance.

claim: All resistance mutants of N. cinerea contained the RplL K84E mutation.
source: In the case of N. cinerea all resistance mutants contained the RplL K84E mutation that we first observed in N. gonorrhoeae, and in the case of N. subflava all resistance mutants contained mutations in dedA (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is genomic sequencing data from resistance mutants of N. cinerea.

claim: All resistance mutants of N. subflava contained mutations in dedA.
source: In the case of N. cinerea all resistance mutants contained the RplL K84E mutation that we first observed in N. gonorrhoeae, and in the case of N. subflava all resistance mutants contained mutations in dedA (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is genomic sequencing data from resistance mutants of N. subflava.

claim: Other Neisseria species likely show higher MICs than N. gonorrhoeae because of either the absence of DedA-assisted uptake or reduced RplL protein oxydifficidin sensitivity.
source: Other Neisseria species likely show higher MICs than N. gonorrhoeae because of either the absence of DedA-assisted uptake or reduced RplL protein oxydifficidin sensitivity.
evidence: This is inferred from the resistance mutation patterns in different Neisseria species.

claim: High oxydifficidin sensitivity results from a combination of DedA-assisted oxydifficidin uptake into the cytoplasm and the presence of an oxydifficidin-sensitive RplL protein.
source: The model that arises from our studies is that high oxydifficidin sensitivity results from a combination of DedA-assisted oxydifficidin uptake into the cytoplasm and the presence of an oxydifficidin-sensitive RplL protein (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is a model inferred from all the experimental data and shown in Figure 3e.

claim: N. gonorrhoeae is uniquely sensitive to oxydifficidin because it contains both DedA-assisted uptake and an oxydifficidin-sensitive RplL protein.
source: N. gonorrhoeae is uniquely sensitive to oxydifficidin because it contains both.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data on DedA and RplL contributions to sensitivity.

claim: DedA is critical to oxydifficidin's potent activity as it sensitizes N. gonorrhoeae to oxydifficidin and decreases its kill time.
source: DedA is critical to oxydifficidin's potent activity as it not only sensitizes N. gonorrhoeae to oxydifficidin but also decreases its kill time, both of which are appealing from a clinical development perspective.
evidence: This is based on MIC and time-kill assay data comparing WT and dedA knockout strains.

claim: Almost 60% of clinically approved antibiotics target the ribosome.
source: Almost 60% of clinically approved antibiotics target the ribosome (Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2021.

claim: Most ribosome-targeting antibiotics inhibit the ribosome by binding to only a small number of sites.
source: Although it is the most common target for natural product antibiotics, most of these molecules inhibit the ribosome by binding to only a small number of sites (Lin et al., 2018; Poehlsgaard and Douthwaite, 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Lin et al., 2018 and Poehlsgaard and Douthwaite, 2005.

claim: Clinically approved antibiotics generally inhibit protein synthesis by binding in either the ribosomal decoding center, peptidyl transfer center, or the peptide exit tunnel.
source: Clinically approved antibiotics generally inhibit protein synthesis by binding in either the ribosomal decoding center, peptidyl transfer center, or the peptide exit tunnel.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ribosome-targeting antibiotics.

claim: Targeting unexploited sites of the ribosome is considered a key step to developing next generation antibiotics that can circumvent existing antibiotic resistance mechanisms.
source: Targeting unexploited sites of the ribosome is considered a key step to developing next generation antibiotics that can circumvent the existing antibiotic resistance mechanisms.
evidence: This is established knowledge in antibiotic development.

claim: Oxydifficidin has a distinct binding site in the ribosome compared to other clinically used antibiotics.
source: Our data suggest that oxydifficidin has a distinct binding site in the ribosome compared to other clinically used antibiotics making it an appealing therapeutic candidate.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of cross-resistance with other ribosome-targeting antibiotics.

claim: The frequency of mutations in either dedA or rplL in N. gonorrhoeae was quite low (~10^-9).
source: In our resistance mutant screening experiments with N. gonorrhoeae the frequency of mutations in either dedA or rplL was quite low (~10–9).
evidence: This is based on the resistance mutation screening data.

claim: The dedA deletion mutant exhibited altered cell morphology, characterized by diminished membrane integrity and reduced micro-colony formation.
source: The dedA deletion mutant exhibited altered cell morphology, characterized by diminished membrane integrity and reduced micro-colony formation (Appendix 1—figure 4), indicating that it should show reduced pathogenesis and fitness, and, as a result, not accumulate in a clinical setting, which adds to the therapeutic appeal of oxydifficidin.
evidence: This is based on microscopy data shown in Appendix 1—figure 4.

claim: The dedA deletion mutant should show reduced pathogenesis and fitness.
source: The dedA deletion mutant exhibited altered cell morphology, characterized by diminished membrane integrity and reduced micro-colony formation (Appendix 1—figure 4), indicating that it should show reduced pathogenesis and fitness, and, as a result, not accumulate in a clinical setting, which adds to the therapeutic appeal of oxydifficidin.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed morphological defects.

claim: dedA mutants should not accumulate in a clinical setting.
source: The dedA deletion mutant exhibited altered cell morphology, characterized by diminished membrane integrity and reduced micro-colony formation (Appendix 1—figure 4), indicating that it should show reduced pathogenesis and fitness, and, as a result, not accumulate in a clinical setting, which adds to the therapeutic appeal of oxydifficidin.

claim: Reexamining old sources through the lens of today's most important pathogens may be a productive approach for identifying therapeutically appealing antibiotics.
source: While most natural product research efforts are focused on identifying novel chemical entities, the work presented here suggests that reexamining old sources through the lens of today's most important pathogens may also be a productive approach for identifying therapeutically appealing antibiotics.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the discovery of oxydifficidin's specific activity.

claim: Increasing rates of antibiotic resistance present a significant clinical threat as they have the potential of rendering gonorrhea infections untreatable.
source: Increasing rates of antibiotic resistance present a significant clinical threat as they have the potential of rendering gonorrhea infections untreatable.
evidence: This is established knowledge about antibiotic resistance.

claim: The recent appearance of N. gonorrhoeae 'superbugs' with high-level resistance to all currently recommended drugs treating gonorrhea infections is particularly concerning.
source: The recent appearance of N. gonorrhoeae 'superbugs' with high-level resistance to all currently recommended drugs treating gonorrhea infections, is particularly concerning (Ohnishi et al., 2011; Day et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ohnishi et al., 2011 and Day et al., 2022.

claim: Oxydifficidin showed activity in an animal model.
source: One appealing feature in the original reports of the discovery of oxydifficidin was its activity in an animal model, a key hurdle for many natural products (Zimmerman et al., 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zimmerman et al., 1987.

claim: Oxydifficidin's clinical significance was limited because of the weak activity it exhibited against most bacterial pathogens.

claim: Oxydifficidin is specifically potent against N. gonorrhoeae including multidrug-resistant N. gonorrhoeae.
source: Our identification of oxydifficidin as being specifically potent against N. gonorrhoeae including multidrug-resistant N. gonorrhoeae, provides a potential new path forward for this structurally interesting natural antibiotic.
evidence: This is based on MIC testing data shown in Figure 1c and Table 1.

claim: Oxydifficidin is active against both wild-type and multidrug-resistant N. gonorrhoeae.
source: Oxydifficidin is active against both wild-type and multidrug-resistant N. gonorrhoeae.

claim: Oxydifficidin's potent activity results from a combination of DedA-assisted uptake into the cytoplasm and the presence of an oxydifficidin-sensitive ribosomal protein L7/L12 (RplL).
source: Its potent activity results from a combination of DedA-assisted uptake into the cytoplasm and the presence of an oxydifficidin-sensitive ribosomal protein L7/L12 (RplL).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on all the experimental data on DedA and RplL.

claim: Oxydifficidin binds to the ribosome at a site that is distinct from other antibiotics.
source: Our data indicate that oxydifficidin binds to the ribosome at a site that is distinct from other antibiotics and that L7/L12 is uniquely associated with its mode of action.
